items.stem_md:
**Community Garden**

Three years ago, the empty land behind Suan Mai School was full of rubbish. Today, it is a community garden where students and neighbors grow vegetables together. The idea came from a group of Grade 10 students who were tired of seeing plastic bags blowing across the field. At first, many adults doubted that teenagers could keep the project going. However, the students organized a weekly schedule, asked a local farmer for advice, and sold their vegetables at the school market. The money they earned was used to buy seeds and tools. Now, more than forty families take part, and the garden has become a place where older and younger people share knowledge. Several other schools in the province have visited to learn how to start similar projects.

---

What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Students sold the vegetables they grew at the school market every week to earn money for the project.
School gardening should become part of the national curriculum.
Adults did not trust teenagers to do anything useful.
Students created a garden that unites the community.

items.stem_md:
**Sleep and Learning**

Many teenagers believe that staying up late to study will help them get better grades. Sleep researchers, however, suggest the opposite. When we sleep, the brain sorts and stores the information we learned during the day. Students who sleep less than six hours a night often find it harder to concentrate and remember facts. In one classroom activity, two groups of students learned the same list of words. One group was tested after eight hours of sleep, while the other was tested after spending the same amount of time awake. The sleeping group remembered more words. This does not mean that studying is unimportant. Rather, it shows that sleep is part of learning, not a break from it. Experts recommend that teenagers get eight to ten hours of sleep and avoid using phones for at least an hour before bed.

---

Which is the best title for the passage?
choices: A Study About Remembering Words
How to Get Better Grades in Every Subject
The Dangers of Using Phones
Why Sleep Matters for Learning

**Floating Market**

For more than sixty years, Riverside Floating Market was mainly a place where farmers sold fruit to local families. When a popular travel program featured the market in 2015, everything changed. Within a few months, weekend visitors increased from a few hundred to several thousand. Some vendors were delighted because their income doubled. Others were less happy. They complained that parking spaces were always full and that traditional wooden boats were being replaced by larger, noisier ones. The local council eventually introduced a rule limiting the number of motorboats. Today, the market tries to balance its new popularity with its old way of life.

---

**The Two-Minute Rule**

Many people feel overwhelmed by long to-do lists. One simple technique that can help is the two-minute rule. The idea is that if a task takes less than two minutes, such as replying to a short message or putting a book back on the shelf, you should do it immediately instead of writing it down. This prevents small tasks from piling up and makes your list look less frightening. For bigger tasks, the rule suggests starting with just two minutes of work, because getting started is often the hardest part.

---

Which is the best title?
choices: How to Reply to Messages Quickly
A Simple Rule for Getting Things Done
Why People Hate To-Do Lists
The Long History of Time Management Around the World

The school library will host a repair café on Saturday from 9 a.m. to noon. Students may bring one broken household item, such as a lamp, fan, or small radio. Volunteer technicians will first check whether the item is safe to open. They will then show its owner how to identify the fault and, when possible, replace a simple part. Places are limited to thirty items, so visitors should collect a numbered card at the library entrance.

It will review bottle sales again before deciding whether to install a third station.

items.stem_md:
**Trying the Quiet Carriage**

I tried the new quiet carriage on the town's electric bus during my trip home. The sign at the door asks passengers to silence phones and keep conversations brief, but it does not ban all sound. At first, the carriage was calm enough for me to finish two chapters of a book. Halfway through the trip, however, a recorded stop announcement became unusually loud. The driver later explained that the volume had been raised temporarily because the rear speaker was not working. I still found the service useful, especially for reading, although calling it “quiet” may create expectations that the operator cannot always meet. A better name might be “low-conversation carriage,” along with a notice that safety announcements will remain audible.

---

What is the reviewer's overall view?
choices: The carriage is useful, but its name may promise more quiet than it can deliver
The current name is accurate because the carriage stayed quiet throughout the trip
The carriage is useful only if recorded safety announcements are removed
The service should keep its name but allow longer conversations instead of announcements

items.stem_md:
**How to Use the Seed Exchange**

The seed exchange cabinet lets students share seeds from vegetables, herbs, and flowers. To contribute, place dry seeds in a paper envelope and write the plant name, the month collected, and basic growing conditions on the front. Do not use a sealed plastic bag, because moisture trapped inside can cause mold. Put the envelope in the “New Seeds” tray rather than directly in a drawer. A garden club member checks new envelopes every Wednesday and then files them by plant type. To take seeds, choose one envelope and record its code in the notebook beside the cabinet. You may take only part of the contents; leave enough for another person and close the envelope. Seeds with no label or signs of mold will be removed.

---

What is the guide mainly about?
choices: How club members choose which seeds students may buy
Why sealed plastic bags protect seeds better than paper envelopes
How to grow vegetables inside the exchange cabinet
How to contribute and take seeds safely and fairly

items.stem_md:
**Why the Afternoon Bus Runs Late**

The student council reviewed thirty days of arrival records for the afternoon activity bus. The bus reached the final stop more than ten minutes late on twelve days. At first, students blamed heavy traffic near the market. The records showed a different pattern: on nine of those twelve days, departure from school had already been delayed because clubs submitted passenger lists after the 4 p.m. deadline. Traffic added time on some days, but it was not the main repeated cause. Starting next week, club leaders must submit names by 3:45 p.m., and the driver will receive one combined list at 4 p.m. The council will compare the next thirty days with the earlier records before deciding whether the new deadline works.

---

What is the report mainly about?
choices: The driver delayed departure while checking a list submitted on time
Records identified late passenger lists as the main repeated cause of bus delays
The bus was more than ten minutes late on most of the thirty days
Traffic near the market caused each recorded delay

items.stem_md:
**Rooftop Garden Watering Notice**

The rooftop garden team measured the soil at 4 p.m. for four days.

| Day | Soil reading | Rain since noon | Action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Monday | 28% | 0 mm | Watered |
| Tuesday | 46% | 7 mm | Not watered |
| Wednesday | 31% | 0 mm | Watered |
| Thursday | 43% | 2 mm | Not watered |

For this trial, the team waters only when the reading is below 35%. Rainfall is recorded to help explain the reading, but rain alone does not decide the action. Next week, the team will move one sensor away from the wall because water dripping from the roof may make that spot wetter than the rest of the bed. Until then, volunteers should follow the soil reading shown on the shared display rather than judge by touching the top layer.

---

What is the notice mainly about?
choices: Using rainfall records alone to decide whether the garden needs water
Confirming that the sensor beside the wall represents the whole bed accurately
Using soil readings to guide watering and improve the trial
Letting volunteers replace measured readings with a touch test

items.stem_md:
**A Second Life for Stage Costumes**

School plays often require costumes that are worn only once. This term, the drama club opened a shared costume closet to give those clothes a second life. Before an item enters the closet, two students check that it is clean, label its size, and photograph any existing damage. Borrowers reserve items in a notebook and return them within three school days after a performance. In the first six weeks, forty-two items were borrowed, and only one came back late. The closet has saved money, but its less obvious benefit is creative: students have begun adapting old pieces instead of copying costumes they see online. The club plans to add a small repair table, although it will not accept items that cannot be washed safely.

---

What is the article mainly about?
choices: A costume closet that photographs damage only after an item is returned late
A sharing system that saves resources and encourages creative reuse
A rental service that accepts hard-to-wash costumes and charges for a repair table
A sharing system that saves money by asking borrowers to copy costumes they find online

**Museum Audio Tour Update**

The town museum has revised its self-guided audio tour after visitors reported that the old version moved too quickly. The new tour contains twelve short tracks instead of one continuous recording. Each track begins beside a numbered blue label, so visitors can pause, skip an object, or change the order. Four tracks include optional descriptions of colors and shapes for visitors who cannot see the displays clearly. Printed transcripts are available at the front desk, but they follow the standard order and do not include the optional descriptions. The museum recommends headphones, although a small number can be borrowed with an identification card. The tour is free with admission and takes about thirty-five minutes if every track is played.

---

What is the announcement mainly about?
choices: A revised audio tour that adds a separate listening fee and requires personal headphones
A more flexible and accessible version of the museum's audio tour
A revised audio tour that requires visitors to play its tracks in one fixed order
A revised audio tour whose printed transcript contains more descriptions than the recordings

items.stem_md:
**Students Monitor the Creek**

A science class has begun monitoring the creek behind the sports field after students noticed that the water sometimes turned cloudy following rain. Every Monday morning, teams measure temperature and clarity at three marked points. They also photograph the banks, but they do not enter the water or collect animals. After five weeks, the class found that clarity usually dropped at the point below a bare patch of soil, while the two upstream points changed less. This pattern does not prove that the soil caused the cloudy water, so the students will place straw on half of the bare patch and compare the next five weeks of readings. If clarity improves only below the covered half, they will have stronger evidence before proposing a permanent solution.

---

What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Students are collecting and testing evidence about cloudy creek water
The school has permanently covered the entire bank with straw
The class is learning to catch animals in the water
Students have already proved who polluted the creek
